title: Norway Hits Pause on Data Centres
topic: Allocating scarce grid capacity between data centres
hook: Norway's grid operator has 800 MW of data centres connected, 4,200 MW reserved and 9,100 MW queued. Then it hit pause. Who gets the next megawatt?
tension: Norway wants data-centre investment but cannot connect everything requested without risking grid stability, and fairness to those already in the queue limits how it can choose.
disclosure: Educational case built from public reporting as of November 10, 2026. It is not legal, investment or policy advice, and the rules described were still being drafted.
brief: On Monday, November 9, 2026, Norway's grid operator Statnett said it was temporarily stopping new grid-capacity reservations for data centres. As of November 10, 2026, the pause runs until new technical requirements are approved by the regulator, and no later than August 1, 2027.

The reason is stability as much as supply. Large data centres can change their power use very quickly, which Statnett says creates challenges for stable operation of the grid. The requirements it is preparing cover when a data centre must stay connected during grid disturbances, how fast consumption may ramp up or down, and how to limit oscillations in the grid. The government announced a licensing scheme for existing and future data centres the same day.

The pause is not a general ban. Existing connections are unaffected, facilities that already have approved functional requirements can still connect, and regional-grid applications that are close to completion keep moving. Statnett also says it will not reassign capacity if that would disadvantage data centres ahead in the queue, and that it applies the measure in a neutral and non-discriminatory way.

The numbers explain the pressure. Data centres have 800 MW connected, 4,200 MW reserved and 9,100 MW in the connection queue, plus a further 18,000 MW of requests. Norway's peak national demand is a little over 25,000 MW. Reporting by Nordisk Post says ministers want new rules to favour facilities that provide essential services such as defence, healthcare and telecom, and are examining whether industry could help finance new generation, such as offshore wind, or whether the state should take stakes in projects judged especially valuable.
Industry groups warn that changing the rules could weaken investor confidence, and Google has said further expansion at one of its Norwegian sites could depend on the forthcoming rules.

question.text: You advise the working group that must draft the rule for who gets grid capacity once the pause ends. Statnett must stay neutral, queue positions matter, and the stability requirements are still being written. Recommend the allocation rule you would put in front of the minister, and defend it.

parts.label: Name the constraint
parts.prompt: What is actually scarce: megawatts, grid stability, or something else? Use two figures from the exhibits.

parts.label: Your allocation rule
parts.prompt: Who gets capacity first, on what condition, and what happens to capacity that is reserved but unused? Be specific enough that Statnett could apply it.

parts.label: Who loses
parts.prompt: Name who is worse off under your rule, the investor-confidence risk the industry has raised, and one step that reduces it.

parts.label: How you would know
parts.prompt: Give two signals you would track after launch and the result that would make you change the rule.

rubric.name: Diagnosis of the constraint
rubric.measures: Whether the answer separates the volume problem (generation and transmission) from the stability problem (fast, unpredictable load swings).
rubric.excellent: Names both scarcities, says which one the pause targets, and uses two figures correctly to show requests cannot all be served.
rubric.weak: Says only that there is not enough power, or restates the figures without saying what they imply.

rubric.name: A rule Statnett could apply
rubric.measures: Whether the rule has an ordering principle, conditions, and a way to deal with reserved capacity that goes unused.
rubric.excellent: States who goes first and why, attaches checkable conditions or milestones, respects queue positions or explains the exception, and says what happens to released capacity.
rubric.weak: Offers a vague priority such as favouring important projects, with no test, decision-maker or treatment of the existing queue.

rubric.name: Use of the numbers
rubric.measures: Whether figures are used correctly and where they matter, across all parts.
rubric.excellent: Uses at least two figures correctly, separates connected from reserved from requested, and does the comparison with peak demand without error.
rubric.weak: Treats all requests as real demand, mixes megawatts with energy, or misstates a figure.

rubric.name: Trade-offs and investor confidence
rubric.measures: Whether the answer is honest about who loses and deals with the investor-confidence risk raised by industry groups.
rubric.excellent: Names the specific losers, explains why confidence is at risk, and proposes a concrete mitigation such as grandfathering or publishing criteria early.
rubric.weak: Claims the rule is fair to everyone, or names a risk with no response to it.

rubric.name: Measurability and a trigger to change course
rubric.measures: Whether the answer chooses signals that can be observed and says what result would change the rule.
rubric.excellent: Two observable signals tied to the rule's goals and a clear trigger for revising it.
rubric.weak: Generic signals such as success or satisfaction, with no trigger.

model_answer.summary: Keep queue order, but make reservations use-it-or-lose-it, and give released capacity to essential services and to projects that bring their own generation or accept flexibility.

parts.text: The total of requests cannot all be served: 32,100 MW of connected, reserved, queued and further requests is about 128% of Norway's peak national demand of a little over 25,000 MW. Two scarcities sit under that number. One is volume, meaning generation and transmission to serve the load. The other is stability, meaning how fast and how unpredictably a data centre's load can swing. The pause targets the second. The talk of financing new generation targets the first.

Honour reservations, but make them earn it. Only 800 MW is connected against 4,200 MW reserved, so unused reservations are the cheapest capacity to free. Keep queue order, because Statnett has said it will not disadvantage those ahead, but attach dated milestones: technical approval under the new stability requirements, a signed power contract, and construction start. A reservation that misses a milestone returns its capacity to a shared pool. Allocate the pool in rounds: first facilities providing essential services such as defence, healthcare and telecom, then projects that bring new generation or accept ramp limits and curtailment.

Speculative developers who reserved without a ready project lose, and so do later entrants with no essential-service claim. The confidence risk is real because the rules change after reservations were made. Reduce it by grandfathering every reservation that meets its milestones, publishing the criteria and the timetable well before the pause ends, no later than August 1, 2027, and giving near-ready projects a clear route in.

Track the share of reserved capacity that meets its milestones versus is released, and the time from approval to energisation. Change the rule if the shared pool stays empty because reservations are never released, or if essential-service projects crowd out everything else for a full allocation round.

alternatives.option: Pure queue order with technical requirements only
alternatives.better_when: Speed and legal certainty matter most and generation is not the binding limit.

alternatives.option: An auction or pay-to-connect scheme that funds new generation
alternatives.better_when: New generation is the binding limit and the state wants the industry to pay for it.

alternatives.option: State-led selection of a few strategic projects, possibly with state stakes
alternatives.better_when: The aim is a handful of nationally valuable projects rather than a broad market.

common_traps.trap: Writing as a data-centre operator asking for capacity
common_traps.why: The role is the allocator. The answer must be a rule that treats applicants even-handedly, not a pitch for one of them.

common_traps.trap: Treating the 32,100 MW of requests as real demand
common_traps.why: Reservations and requests are options on capacity. Only 800 MW is connected. A good answer separates intent from load and plans for attrition.

Statnett has said it will not reassign capacity to the disadvantage of those ahead in the queue and that it applies the pause neutrally. A rule that jumps the queue without a reason invites a challenge.
That may be right in the long run, but the decision is who gets scarce capacity when the pause ends, no later than August 1, 2027.

common_traps.trap: A priority list with no mechanism
common_traps.why: 'Prioritise important projects' cannot be applied. Say who decides, on what test, and what happens to unused reservations.
